meanings.note: The main Levantine verb for 'talk / say / tell', far more common in Amman than تكلم.

examples.trans: Who told you the news?
Tell me what happened with you.

meanings.note: Appears in the everyday adverbial phrase بالضبط (pronounced biz-zabt in Jordan), meaning 'exactly'.

examples.trans: Tell me what happened exactly.
That is exactly what I mean.

meanings.note: Core Levantine question word for 'what?' (شو صار؟) and casual conversation starter ('So, ...').

examples.trans: What are you doing here?
So, ready to go?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'do' or 'make' (بعمل وظيفة 'doing homework', بعملوا مشاكل 'making trouble').

examples.trans: How did you do on the exam?
I didn't do anything wrong.

meanings.note: At AlRawabi, الساحة is the central open courtyard where students gather.

examples.trans: We went down to the courtyard at recess.
The girls are standing in the middle of the courtyard.

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.

examples.trans: Come here, Mariam.
Thank you very much, Miss.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.

examples.trans: I didn't hear the bell.
Come before the school closes.

meanings.note: In the past مع ما (ما عرفت شو أعمل), means 'I didn't know what to do'; b-present بعرف means 'I know'.

examples.trans: I know this place well.
I didn't know how to answer the question.

meanings.note: Versatile noun: ما عندي وقت ('no time'), صار الوقت ('it's time'), وقتها ('at that moment / then'), مش وقته ('not the time for it').

examples.trans: I didn't have time to explain.
Everything is nice in its own time.

meanings.note: Standard Jordanian private-school address for a female teacher or principal, used alone (يا مس) or before her first name (مس فاتن، مس عبير).

examples.trans: Yes Miss, I'm ready.
Ms. Faten is in her office now.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine counterpart of ظل; before another verb (يضل يتحمل، بتضلك تخططي) it means 'keep on doing'.

examples.trans: I stayed at school until afternoon.
You keep asking the same question.

meanings.note: Active participle of سكت: ضليت ساكتة ('I stayed silent').

examples.trans: Why are you sitting quietly?
We stayed silent the whole class.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings directly in speech: لإني ('because I'), لإنها ('because she').

examples.trans: I stayed home because I was tired.
I apologized because I was late.

meanings.note: Past tense linking verb (كنت، كنتي، كان، كنا) and subjunctive تكون / نكون ('to be'); ما كان عندي means 'I didn't have'.

examples.trans: I was at school in the morning.
Today was very long.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word (pronounced ktiir) used before or after adjectives ('very') and after plural nouns ('many').

examples.trans: The movie was really good.
I have lots of friends at school.

meanings.note: Active participle of خاف, very common in speech for 'feeling scared right now' (كنت خايفة).

examples.trans: I was very scared at the time.
I'm afraid you'll tell someone.

meanings.note: Everyday time conjunction for both past ('when I went down': لما نزلت) and general/future events (لما الإشي يدخل بخطتي).

examples.trans: Call me when you arrive.
I was happy when I saw you.

meanings.note: Means both 'get off' a vehicle (انزلي من الباص) and 'go down' to the schoolyard (نزلت عالساحة).

examples.trans: We went down to the courtyard together.
Get off the bus calmly.

meanings.note: Used with manner phrases like بشكل طبيعي ('in a normal way') or بطبيعتك ('naturally').

examples.trans: I acted calmly in front of everyone.
Act naturally.

meanings.note: With بـ + adjective, بشكل forms manner adverbs: بشكل طبيعي ('in a normal way / naturally').

examples.trans: She acted in a calm way.
She solved the problem in a smart way.

meanings.note: Plural طبيعيين ('normal people'); بشكل طبيعي means 'normally / casually'.

examples.trans: That is a very natural feeling.
I acted in a normal way.

meanings.note: Sets up an unexpected turn in a story (فجأة ليان إجت).

examples.trans: Suddenly everyone in the classroom went quiet.
She appeared in front of me suddenly.

meanings.note: Core Levantine verb for 'come': past إجيت / إجت, b-present باجي / بتيجي.

examples.trans: Why didn't you come yesterday?
Next time I'll come with you.

meanings.note: With object suffix مسكتني ('she grabbed me').

examples.trans: She held my hand and we walked together.
Layan grabbed me by my shoulder.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings مني (from me), منها (of/from her), منكم (of you): تكون من شلتها ('be part of her clique'), بخاف منها ('afraid of her').

examples.trans: I got off the bus.
Which one of you saw what happened?

meanings.note: Spoken form of وراء: spatial 'behind' (ماشيين وراها، من ورا 'from behind') and sequential 'one after another' (واحدة ورا الثانية).

examples.trans: I sat at the desk behind you.
They walked into class one after another.

meanings.note: Independent first-person singular pronoun for any gender.

examples.trans: I am a student at the school.
I didn't say anything.

meanings.note: Versatile Levantine word meaning 'but' between clauses and 'only / just' inside a clause.
As a focus adverb before a verb, noun, or imperative, بس narrows or softens the statement.

examples.trans: I tried to speak, but she didn't hear me.
I just want one minute.

meanings.note: Levantine 'want' built from بد- plus pronoun suffixes: بدي (I want), بدك (you want), بدنا (we want).

examples.trans: What do you want to do now?
I wanted to talk with you.

meanings.note: Covers transitive 'push someone away' (أبعدها عني) and the everyday imperative ابعدي ('step away').

examples.trans: Step out of my way.
I wanted to push her away from me.

meanings.note: Marks topics (عني 'about me'), distance (ابعدي عن طريقي 'away from my path'), and defense (بيدافعوا عنها 'defend her').

examples.trans: We talked about the movie yesterday.
Stay away from her, please.

meanings.note: Everyday oath used earnestly to swear one is telling the truth (والله ما حكيت إشي) or surprisedly in والله جد؟ ('oh really?').

examples.trans: I swear I'm telling the truth.
Honestly, I'm glad to see you.

meanings.note: With pronoun suffixes: ما كان قصدي ('I didn't mean to') and شو قصدك؟ ('what do you mean?').

examples.trans: I swear I didn't mean to upset you.
What do you mean by this question?

meanings.note: Used in Jordanian speech with subjunctive forms like أأذيها ('hurt her') and يأذوا ('they hurt').

examples.trans: I didn't mean to hurt you.
They won't hurt anyone.

meanings.note: Invariable modal word followed by a subjunctive verb (لازم نتحمل، مش لازم نلفت نظرهم).

examples.trans: We have to go to class now.
We mustn't talk loudly.

meanings.note: Form II verb (saddaq, written here with shadda to distinguish it from the noun صدق 'honesty'): أصدقك ('believe you'), لا تصدقوها ('don't believe her').

examples.trans: You have to believe me, Miss.
Nobody believed her lie.

meanings.note: Intensive adjective/noun; feminine كذابة! ('she's a liar!').

examples.trans: Don't believe him, he's a liar.
She called her a liar in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: Emphasizes contrast in cleft sentences like هي اللي بلشت ('she is the one who started it').

examples.trans: She has been my friend since childhood.
She doesn't move without them.

meanings.note: Invariable Levantine relative pronoun replacing الذي / التي / الذين and 'what' (اللي صار 'what happened').

examples.trans: The girl whom I saw is my friend.
Tell me what happened.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine verb for starting something or starting a fight (هي اللي بلشت 'she's the one who started it').

examples.trans: Class started a little while ago.
Who started the problem?

meanings.note: With an object suffix (ضربتني 'she hit me'), marks direct physical aggression.

examples.trans: She is the one who hit me first.
The bell rang a little while ago.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine preposition taking nouns (قدام المديرة) or suffixes (قدامهم 'in front of them').

examples.trans: She stood in front of the whole class.
Act normal in front of them.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, كل means 'every' (كل يوم، كل إشي); with الـ (الكل) it means 'everyone'; with suffixes (كلنا، كلهم، كلها) 'all of us/them/it'.

examples.trans: Everyone knows the story.
We see each other every day.

meanings.note: Imperative feminine اهدي ('calm down!') and plural اهدوا ('calm down, everyone!').

examples.trans: Calm down a bit and take a breath.
Things calmed down after the argument.

meanings.note: High-frequency Levantine word for 'now' (contracted from هاد الوقت).

examples.trans: We have to go to class right now.
I feel a bit relieved now.

meanings.note: Used in بدي أفهم القصة كلها ('I want to understand the whole story').

examples.trans: I understood you clearly.
Let me understand what happened.

meanings.note: Refers to an account of events (القصة كلها) or informally to an ongoing drama (بالقصة).

examples.trans: Tell me the story from the beginning.
What's the story with the rooms on the trip?

meanings.note: Two essential senses: 'happen' (اللي صار 'what happened') and 'become / turn into' (صارت كابوس، صار الوقت).

examples.trans: Tell me what happened exactly.
It's time we head to class.

meanings.note: Takes suffixes معي (with me), معك (with you), معها (with her), معنا (with us), معكم (with you all), معهم (with them), and forms مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!').

examples.trans: Come sit with us.
Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

meanings.note: Appears in the classic Arabic farewell مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!', literally 'with safety').

examples.trans: Thank goodness you're safe.
Goodbye, Dina!
